justification: Forming a fresh judgement rather than carrying the round-1 number forward: against the pages that actually rank for 'relational database explained' this article remains decisively ahead, not merely 'fine'. IBM and GeeksforGeeks (both re-fetched this round) top out at definitions and one illustrative query; neither has a worked, requirements-to-schema design problem, neither runs any code, neither discusses NULL-in-a-key engine disagreements, partial unique indexes, or ON DELETE semantics, and neither has an exercise a reader can fail and then check. This article has all of that, backed by 70 executed SQL blocks (run-code passes) and eleven primary documentation sources cited at the specific claim each supports. Distinctive-sentence spot checks turned up no copied or closely paraphrased passages from any competitor or tutorial site (searched verbatim: the heading 'A relation is a set of rows; a table only resembles one', and the sentence about a rejected loan 'landing on a person's desk today instead of surfacing in a report next quarter' -- both return nothing matching, confirming original prose), and the new-this-round Codd quotation about atomic/nondecomposable simple domains checks out as genuinely quoted, not asserted from memory. Round-1's one open finding (the atomic-attribute claim lacking an inline citation) is fixed: the sentence now carries a direct, correctly quoted Codd citation at the point the claim is made. More importantly for an AdSense read, round-1's technical major finding -- that the article's opening promise ('the database enforces [every rule] by itself... no matter which program, script or hurried human sends it') was actually false for half of rule 7, since an ordinary SQLite column let a fractional late fee through -- is also fixed, and fixed honestly rather than papered over: `loan` is now `STRICT`, the fix is demonstrated with a failing insert and a passing edge case (a whole number written as '3.0'), and the closing rule-by-rule summary table was updated to match what is actually enforced. That matters for a low-value-content read specifically because the alternative (declaring victory without re-verifying, or quietly softening the claim without saying why) is the kind of thing this rubric exists to catch, and it did not happen here. Structurally the page still reads nothing like a template: headings compared against the published sibling sql-joins.md ('Three attempts at one report', 'NULL never equals anything, including NULL', 'Anti-joins: finding the rows with no match') and against complexity/big-o-notation.md ('Count the steps before you time anything', 'The definition, with its two constants') share no boilerplate pattern, no repeated Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways shape, and no reused example -- each pillar article owns its own schema, and this one's is the one CONTENT_PLAN explicitly wants reused across the pillar, with sql-joins' deliberately different cut-down schema named and contrasted rather than silently duplicated. No filler openers or closers, no asserted-experience or 'most people think' phrasing, no keyword stuffing, and all internal links (sql-joins, three glossary anchors) resolve to real, existing pages -- no dead ends. docs/crosslinks/databases/relational-model-and-keys.md exists with three sensible pending links, so the missing-sibling-link non-issue still does not apply. I found nothing left to flag: no blocker, major or minor issue from this round's own read, and both prior open findings that touched this role's territory are confirmed fixed. The score moves from round 1's 9.0 to 9.3 because the one concrete gap that kept it off a 'no notes' reading is now closed and re-verified, not because effort was visible -- but it stops short of a 10 because a truly flawless, nothing-else-to-find page at this length and density is a high bar this round's spot checks cannot fully rule out (in particular, the article's other cross-engine 'X and Y and Z all do this' generalizations were sampled, not exhaustively re-verified against every named engine, which is the technical critic's remit rather than this role's).
